newsitem.title: USA: US LPG market relieved after PEMEX Cactus restart.
newsitem.headline: US LPG market relieved after PEMEX Cactus restart.

text.p: The U.S. liquefied petroleum gas market has greeted with a sigh of relief news that Mexico's largest natural gas processing plant has restarted following an explosion last year, traders said.
The Cactus plant in southern Mexico returned on line Thursday at 95 percent of start-up capacity, which Pemex officials rated at 600 million cubic feet per day.

The capacity is one million cubic feet higher than before the July 26, 1996, explosion that killed seven people and severely cut output. Officials said exports of LPGs -- propane and butane, mainly -- may soon resume.
"This removes the fear and anxiety in the U.S. market that caused the huge price increases last winter," said market analyst Dan Lippe of Petral Consulting Co.
"LPG prices in the U.S. won't fall; they just won't rise," Lippe predicted.

Anxiety over the huge supply gap that the explosion carved out in Mexico together with a seasonal rise in demand led to a doubling in propane prices in the Gulf of Mexico from the end July, 1996 to a December peak just above 70 cents a gallon.

The rise came even though much of state-owned PEMEX's needs were met by the international market, with only a small percentage of the replacement barrels actually bought in the U.S. Gulf, according to traders and analysts.
As one Houston trader said: "Pemex's need was always in the back of many player's minds." Rumors continually popped up about Pemex looking for more supply over the last nine months, he said.
Gulf propane came down sharply at the end of December and have been hovering around 35 cents a gallon for the last two months.

The international LPG market too can expect some relief this fall and winter after seeing similar gains last year. Soon after the explosion Pemex snapped up about 20,000 barrels per day of propane from Saudi Arabia in a contract that lasted from September to March.
Though a small amount in terms of the world market, it occured during the winter months when more than 95 percent of supply is contractually committed, said Lippe.

It appears, however, that despite the Cactus start up Pemex is still in need of supply. On Thursday, Pemex was rumored to have bought 30,000 tonnes of propane/butane mix from Saudi Arabia and is currently looking for another butane cargo from an international source, according to traders.

It remains unclear if the barrels are just to put a margin of safety into what are probably low inventory levels at Pemex. Or if the usually tight-lipped monopoly has a greater need than it is letting on.
